items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1976-02-13
items.q: Eddie Miller played there with me for a while. Who's now playing with Pete Fountain.

ctx.x: And then you went and played in the French Quarter for a while, I guess.

I went to work at a cabaret. It was called the Cabarets in those days. It was called the Valencia Cabaret. It was where the Royal Sinesta Hotel is today, on Bourbon Street. And I worked with various little groups, three-piece groups there, from time to time. Some of the musicians I played with there was Chink Morton's son, Chink Morton Jr. Eddie Miller played there with me for a while. Who's now playing with Pete Fountain. Yes. And Eddie played alto sax in those days. He wasn't playing tenor. And Al Hesman, banjo…

Not as a single, Charlie, because I worked with groups there. I went from the Fern dance hall over to a little nightclub or cabaret, they call it in those days, called the Valencia, where the Hilton Inn is supposed to go up today on Bourbon Street. And I worked there with a little three-piece group with Chink Morton's son, who played banjo, and Eddie Miller, who played alto sax in those days. And we had a little three-piece outfit. And, well, from there I went to various places. I don't know if I can get them…

This seems to be something that's always struck me as sort of almost a tradition among New Orleans musicians, the reluctance to leave town. I guess Chicago, almost forced out because of the closing of Storyville, and then we know on the current pop charts, our hurt, you know, for a long time resisted leaving town, and so did Pete Fountain. Have you ever thought about this? Why is that there's such a reluctance on the part of major talents, such as yourself, to leave town? It seems like there are big markets…

Orleanians seem hesitant about going on the road? Well, I would imagine that it is the glamorous atmosphere that New Orleans offers, not money-wise, but certainly it has plenty of atmosphere, and if you're born here, you know what it is. It's just as you say, do you know what it means to miss New Orleans? Well, this is very true, and if you have ever been away for a while, why do you get this urge to come back? And, of course, I was always, as I said, sort of a guy that was stuck close to home, and, well, one…
